title: Six words
hookLine: an epitaph is a life in a line
carry: a life pressed into a line

cards: A small cemetery in Amherst, Massachusetts. A plain stone behind an iron fence, with a name on it, Emily Dickinson, her dates, and just two words: Called Back.
Across an ocean, in a cemetery in Rome, a stone does the opposite. It doesn't give the name at all.
It calls the man beneath it a young English poet, and gives a line he asked for: "Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water." That's John Keats. One stone says almost nothing.
The other leaves out the one thing a gravestone usually gives. Both say a great deal: a life in a line.

teach.b: First, what an epitaph is for. It's a life pressed into a line and cut into stone, and it isn't for the dead. It's for whoever walks by later: a grandchild, a stranger, someone looking for shade.
It answers one question for them: who was this?
Second, Called Back. Dickinson's stone holds just those words under her name and dates, and it's said she used them in one of her last notes to her cousins.
Some readers hear a summons, someone being called home; others hear something quieter, like a child called in from playing at dusk. The stone doesn't explain.
Third, a name writ in water. Keats, dying young and, by his friends' account, sure his poems would be forgotten, asked for that line and no name.

His friends kept the name off, though they added bitter words of their own about his enemies above it. Water doesn't hold writing. People still walk to his grave to read the line about vanishing, its own small irony.
Fourth, six words, because six is short enough to force a choice. Not a résumé, not a list of jobs: what would you want someone in the shade to know?
That closes a week of grief: waves that come and go, a bond that continues, love for an animal that was real, grief before and after, plain words for children, rites that hold us.
And now the shortest thing a life can leave: six words.

how: Families choose epitaphs with care: sometimes a line of scripture, a favorite phrase, or a few words that sum up a life, and some people write their own long before they're needed.

o: a rule limiting what a gravestone may say
a whole life pressed into one short line

s: Keats's stone in Rome carries his name in large letters
it leaves his name off and calls him a young English poet.
just those words, under her name and dates.
an epitaph is mainly written for the dead
it's for whoever walks by later.

games.q: you get one line on your stone, six words. what goes on it?
o: a list of your job titles.
something about what you loved, or how you lived.
games.why: neither Dickinson nor Keats listed achievements. a line about how you lived is the one a stranger in the shade can carry.

practice: Let a few words come about the life you're actually living, not the one on paper, and try one line of six, counting them on your fingers. Too many, cut one; not quite true, change it; it can be funny, plain, or a little odd.
When one fits, say it once in your head, and let it rest.

wordCard.voice: Six words: a life pressed into one short line, the way an epitaph speaks to whoever walks by later. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a life pressed into a line. Six words can hold more than they seem. Day eight hundred five closes the week.
